Q: How to customize Slider ticks in a visual way A:

Short answer

After some testing, my conclusion is that the only way that slider ticks can be visually customized is to change their distribution along the slider track, in other words, to change the spacing of the ticks.

Unfortunately, it seems it is not possible to customize the actual appearance of the tick marks.

Customizing the distribution of the tick marks

When the init variant with a tick parameter is used, the closure that builds the ticks is called for every step value. Inside the closure, the value that is supplied to SliderTick determines the position of the tick along the track. If this value is different to the step value, the step value still takes effect. So this allows the spacing to be customized.

Here is an example that shows isolated ticks for values that are multiples of 10, but clusters of ticks for the values in-between:

struct ContentView: View {
    @State private var value = 0.0

    var body: some View {
        Slider(
            value: $value,
            in: 0...50,
            step: 1,
            label: { Text("Value") },
            tick: { val in
                let remainder = Int(val) % 10
                let skewedVal = remainder > 0 ? val + (Double(5 - remainder) / 2) : val
                return SliderTick(skewedVal)
            }
        )
        .padding(.horizontal)
        .padding(.vertical, 40)
        .overlay(alignment: .top) {
            Text(String(format: "%.1f", value))
        }
    }
}

Here is another example with a range of 0...10 that distributes the tick marks based on the square of the value:

Slider(
    value: $value,
    in: 0...10,
    step: 1,
    label: { Text("Value") },
    tick: { val in
        SliderTick(val * val / 10)
    }
)

If the tick marks need to be shown at arbitrary positions then the init variant taking the parameter ticks can be used. This init variant does not have a step. The following example shows ticks at both ends of the track and at 3 other arbitrary positions:

Slider(
    value: $value,
    in: 0...10,
    label: { Text("Value") },
    ticks: {
        SliderTickContentForEach([0.0, 1.2, 2.7, 6.8, 10.0], id: \.self) { val in
            SliderTick(val)
        }
    }
)

Note that the thumb button will always snap to the tick positions. So when ticks for arbitrary values are used, the slider can only be used to select one of the arbitrary values, intermediate values cannot be selected.

Bug alert: When I tested this with VoiceOver on an iPhone running iOS 26.5, the increment and decrement actions caused the value to go up and down in steps of 1. The thumb button snapped to the nearest tick, but the underlying value was a rounded integer. This would seem to me to be a bug. I don't know if there would be ways to prevent the issue by using accessibility modifiers.

Other observations

  • Tick marks are not shown if the init variant init(value:in:step:onEditingChanged:) is used, even though this specifies a step. In order for tick marks to be shown, it is necessary to use an init variant that also defines the label for the slider. AFAIK, the dependency of tick marks on the definition of a slider label is not documented.
  • With iOS, the label for the slider is never displayed, but it is read by VoiceOver. See SwiftUI Slider's label visibility for more discussion.
  • When tick marks are shown, it is not possible to hide individual tick marks. As demonstrated in the question, when the init variant with a tick parameter is used, a tick mark is still shown even when the closure returns nil.
  • Tick marks can be given a position that is off screen, which of course means they will not be seen. However, this doesn't help much, because it makes the associated values unselectable. The thumb button cannot be positioned in a gap along the track that is created using this technique.
  • Multiple ticks cannot be associated with the same value. This causes errors in the console.
  • With iOS, labels for tick marks are never displayed. However, they are displayed on macOS, if defined.

Q: Fusing row with previous row(s) depending on criteria A:

Based on your answer, my previous answer is a little overwrought since you're dumping back to CSV and not doing any further processing, plus you don't actually need the original index. But the approach is still good. So consider this a simpler variation.

Here I'm treating everything as str dtype and I only need to specify one agg function.

df = pd.read_csv("input.csv", sep=";", dtype='str')

(
    df.groupby(df['A date'].notna().cumsum(), as_index=False)
    .agg(lambda items: ' '.join(filter(pd.notna, items)))
)

       A date B string C string D string E integer F integer
0  08.01.2026    a d e        b      c f       3,7          
1  08.01.2026        g        h    i j k      2,11          
2  31.01.2026        l        m        n       8,0          
3  03.02.2026        o      p r      q s                 4,9

Q: Spatial decomposition on non-uniform grid A:

" the interpolation noticeably smooths small-scale features and changes the resulting spectrum."

Sounds like there may be something wrong with your interpolation code.

Please post your code and the data for a small part of your grid that shows the smoothing problem. Also post your output from the interpolation and what you expected to get.

How small are the small smoothed details? If they are no bigger than one of the cells in your grid, then they will get smoothed no matter what you do. Google Nyquist frequency

Q: AttributeError: 'NormalizedLandmark' object has no attribute 'landmark' A:

hand_landmark is NormalizedLandmark and it doesn't have landmark because it is single point with x,y,z and you have to use it directly (without inner for-loop):

if LastLandmarks:
    for hand_landmark in LastLandmarks:
        print(f"POINT: {hand_landmark.x:.2f}  {hand_landmark.y:.2f}  {hand_landmark.z:.2f}")
        cv2.circle(frame, (int(hand_landmark.x * w), int(hand_landmark.y * h)), 2, (255, 0, 0), 2)

Or in print_results() you should assign full result

    LastLandmarks = result   # .hand_landmarks[0]

and then you can have nested for-loops (but it needs .hand_landmarks instead .landmarks)

if LastLandmarks:
    for hand_landmarks in LastLandmarks.hand_landmarks:
        for hand_point in hand_landmarks:
            print(f"POINT: {hand_point.x:.2f}  {hand_point.y:.2f}  {hand_point.z:.2f}")
            cv2.circle(frame, (int(hand_point.x * w), int(hand_point.y * h)), 2, (255, 0, 0), 2)

Doc for NormalizedLandmark

Q: How can I avoid using LLMs as a software developer? A:

in my case no-one questioned my productivity and therefore I have no productivity issue to be fixed at this moment of time.

The productivity issue you have is that management will want you to do 10x what you did without AI. And if you did 4x more than the other developers without AI, it's just simple arithmetic to understand that you, sir, must be doing 40x what other developers did, because that's what the AI salesmen told your managers.

Now, the question is: are your managers those kinds of managers? Are they really expecting a massive boost in your productivity compared to pre-AI? I think it's sarcastic to expect "40x", of course, but your managers really might want to see you become more productive than your previous non-AI-using self.

'Tis the world we live in.
